reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: A hypertrophic scar is raised, red, and often itchy but remains confined within the boundaries of the original wound, unlike a keloid which extends beyond the wound margins
Hypertrophic scars typically appear within weeks of injury and tend to improve or partially regress over months to years, whereas keloids persist and often recur
Risk is increased by wounds under tension, wounds crossing joints or perpendicular to skin tension lines, delayed healing, infection, and burns
Prevention centres on meticulous wound closure, tension reduction, and avoiding infection and delayed healing
First-line management commonly includes silicone gel sheeting, pressure therapy, and scar massage, with intralesional corticosteroid injection for thicker or symptomatic scars
Adjuncts such as laser therapy and, in selected cases, surgical revision can improve appearance, though surgery alone risks recurrence without additional measures
Burn scars are particularly prone to hypertrophy and contracture, and early pressure garments and physiotherapy help limit deformity
Realistic counselling about the prolonged and often incomplete nature of scar improvement is important for patient expectations
reference.pathophysiology: Hypertrophic scarring reflects a dysregulated wound-healing response in which the proliferative phase is prolonged and remodelling is impaired. Excessive and persistent inflammation drives fibroblast proliferation and overproduction of collagen, with an imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown. The collagen is deposited in comparatively organised bundles aligned parallel to the skin surface, distinguishing it histologically from the thick, disorganised collagen of keloids. Mechanical tension across the wound and prolonged inflammation from infection or delayed healing promote this fibrotic response, and myofibroblast activity contributes to scar contraction.
additionalDifferentials: Foreign body granuloma within a scar
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment and scar scoring (e.g. Vancouver Scar Scale) for baseline and monitoring
Photographic documentation to track evolution and treatment response
Biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy is suspected
Assessment of joint range of motion when scars cross a joint or cause contracture
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration, or atypical change suggesting malignancy rather than a simple scar
Progressive contracture across a joint causing functional loss
Signs of secondary infection within the scar or wound
reference.prognosis: Hypertrophic scars often mature and flatten over one to two years and generally respond better to conservative therapy than keloids, with a lower recurrence rate after appropriately combined treatment. Outcomes are less favourable for burn-related scars and scars under tension or across joints, which may require ongoing management to prevent contracture.
pitfalls: Confusing a hypertrophic scar with a keloid, leading to inappropriate treatment expectations
Performing surgical revision alone without adjuncts, resulting in recurrence
Delaying preventive measures such as pressure garments in burn scars
Repeated or excessive corticosteroid injection causing skin atrophy, telangiectasia, or hypopigmentation
Overlooking functional contracture while focusing only on cosmetic appearance
